questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where a school reform can reach
questions.learningObjective: identify the limit on a reform that works through money
questions.stem: A writer proposes that a court may examine the books and teaching of a school kept by a family, and asks what the proposal would change in practice. What is the effect?

options.text: Nothing until a family's own money pays for the teaching, so the reach of the court stops with the parents' choice of school

options.misconception: gives the reform a reach nobody proposed, which is the writer's complaint
options.text: Everything at once, since every child in the town would be taught the same lessons in the same classroom each day

options.misconception: hands the case to a body that has no standing where the money is spent
options.text: The parish's duty alone, since a court has no standing against a house that pays for its own lessons

options.misconception: reduces an inspection of what is taught to a question of its price
options.text: The cost of schooling only, since examining a book shows what it costs and never who is taught from it

questions.explanation: The proposal reaches teaching by way of money, so a family that pays for its own lessons keeps its own curriculum and the examination changes nothing until that payment is the court's business; that is the gap the writer has found. The tempting answers either give the reform a reach no one proposed, hand the case to a body that has no standing where the money goes, or reduce an inspection of content to a question of its price.
questions.hint: Ask what the court would have to reach first.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A shop's week in pence
questions.learningObjective: read takings and copies as two measures of one week's trade
questions.stem: A bookseller's ledger for one week shows 1,800 pence of sales: 600 pence from one six-sheet pamphlet sold at twopence, 300 copies, 150 pence from a daily newspaper at a penny, 150 copies, and 1,050 pence of other books and oddments. What does the week show?

options.text: One pamphlet was a third of the money and twice the copies, so the cheap sheet was both the bestseller and the better seller

options.misconception: ranks a daily by how often it appears, which says nothing about how many it sold
options.text: The newspaper was the bestseller, since a daily title that sells every day must out-sell a single sheet

options.misconception: claims price never touched income, when the two totals plainly differ
options.text: Takings and copies ran together, so the price of an item said nothing about how much money it brought in

options.misconception: reads a third as a half and sends the rest of the week to the daily paper
options.text: The six-sheet took half the week's money, and everything else the shop sold came from the daily paper

questions.explanation: Six hundred pence out of eighteen hundred is a third of the money, and three hundred copies against one hundred and fifty is twice the buyers, so the cheap sheet led on both counts and no trade-off between reach and revenue appears in this week at all. The tempting answers rank a daily by its frequency, claim that price never touched income when the two totals plainly differ, and read a third of the takings as a half.
questions.hint: Compare both the pence and the copies before you answer.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a falling price changes the audience
questions.learningObjective: explain what a cheaper and shorter book does to the kind of reader
questions.stem: A new series of books is issued at a third of the price of the standard histories, in short volumes meant to be finished in an evening. What changes first?

options.text: The kind of reader, since a book that can be finished in an evening can be bought by people with little money or little time

options.misconception: names the right change for the wrong reason, which puts the effect before the cause
options.text: The kind of reader, since a cheap book is more likely to be bought twice than a dear one is bought at all

options.misconception: insists the buyers were fixed whatever the price, so nothing could have moved
options.text: Nothing at all, since the buyers of history were always the same people whatever the price of the volume

options.misconception: grants the printer more money without a single new reader, which is not a market at all
options.text: Only the sales, since a lower price raises what a printer takes without bringing anybody new into the shop

questions.explanation: The two changes in the offer, a lower price and a shorter length, both attack the same obstacle, which is not wanting to read but being unable to pay or unable to find the time, so the first thing to move is the audience rather than the volume of sales. The tempting answers repeat the change in the reader for the wrong reason, insist the buyers were fixed whatever the price, or grant the printer more money without a single new reader, and none of that follows from a cheaper shorter book.
questions.hint: Ask what the price and the length have in common.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The second reading of a used book
questions.learningObjective: identify what a second-hand copy changes for a reader
questions.stem: A bookseller buys a chest of books from a household that has moved house, and sells them again a few weeks later. Why does this widen the reading public?

options.text: A used copy costs less than a new one, so a reader who could not pay the first price may still pay the second

options.misconception: substitutes distance for price, which is a difference the two copies do not have
options.text: A used copy is nearer than a new one, so a reader with no time to visit a bookseller's shop can buy one

options.misconception: substitutes completeness for price, and a second copy of the same book is no fuller
options.text: A used copy is more complete, so a reader who could not find the volume he wanted can now find it

options.misconception: substitutes durability for price, which is a difference in the binding and not in the reader
options.text: A used copy is better kept, so a reader who will not lend his own books will buy a second one to keep

questions.explanation: The second-hand copy works on the one obstacle the first purchase had not removed, the price, because a book that has already been read can be offered below what a new one costs while the text is exactly the same, so the reader who was shut out by the price is not shut out now. The tempting answers substitute distance, completeness and durability for price, and each of those is a difference the two copies of the same book do not have.
questions.hint: What is different about a book that has already been read?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two levers on the same trade
questions.learningObjective: choose the measure that removes a cause rather than a symptom
questions.stem: Printers complain that a political sheet is reprinted in every city. Which measure attacks the cause rather than the copies?

options.text: Release the paper, so more sheets can be printed in every city at the price the trade can still afford to pay

options.misconception: watches for the copies afterwards instead of removing what made them possible
options.text: Hire inspectors, so every reprinting is found within a week and its type is broken up

options.misconception: leaves the shortage in place and only narrows the number of places that can use it
options.text: Close the presses, so the one press that is left is the only one with paper to work with

options.misconception: raises the cost of the very sheet whose spread the state wants to stop
options.text: Tax the sheet, so a reprint costs more than a new sheet and the trade turns to the news

questions.explanation: Every city is reprinting because the sheet is worth printing and the paper to print it with is rationed, so a sheet that arrives anywhere can be copied there, and the ration is the reason the copying happens rather than one of its symptoms. The tempting answers watch for the copies afterwards, or close the one source of paper, or raise the cost, and each of those treats the shortage as a thing to police instead of the thing to relieve.
questions.hint: Ask why the sheet can be reprinted at all.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a change in a judgment records
questions.learningObjective: infer a change in legal reasoning from two contrary judgments
questions.stem: A court decides a case one way, and twenty years later decides a similar case the other way, each time giving its reason in writing. What does the pair of judgments show?

options.text: The reasons the court found persuasive have changed, because the second case is settled by weighing, not by repeating a rule

options.misconception: makes a later court the corrector of an earlier one, which the two reasons do not show
options.text: The first court was mistaken, since a later court that disagrees shows the earlier reasoning had no merit

options.misconception: invents a change in the words of the law, which no one in the pair mentions
options.text: The law itself was rewritten, so the later decision merely applies the new words to an old dispute

options.misconception: treats a reversal as copying, which assumes a decision settles the question for good
options.text: The later court was copying, because a court that reverses itself must have been shown the earlier reasoning

questions.explanation: A written reason is an argument, and an argument has to be weighed each time, so two similar cases decided differently on stated grounds record a change in what the judges found persuasive rather than an error caught late or a statute rewritten. The tempting answers make the later court a corrector of the earlier, invent a change in the words of the law, or treat a reversal as copying, and each of those assumes that a decision settles the question for good.
questions.hint: Two cases, two stated reasons. What can have changed?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The cost that limits a poor family's children
questions.learningObjective: explain how parish relief discourages the poor from keeping their own children
questions.stem: A writer argues that a family will not raise more children if it cannot feed them, and blames the foundling hospitals for teaching the poor that children can be left with the parish. Explain the reasoning.

options.text: Once a wage is spent on bringing up a child who dies, the family keeps the next one at home, so the parish pays and the family does not

options.misconception: makes the hospital cheaper, which would help the family rather than discourage it
options.text: Once a hospital takes a child, the family is freed from all cost, so the poor raise many more than they otherwise would

options.misconception: puts the cost of a child where it is least, so the limit on the number never moves
options.text: Once a hospital is built, the food it buys is cheaper, so the poor can afford more children than they did before

options.misconception: blames the family's industry, which the writer's account of the cost does not raise
options.text: Once the parish pays, the poor refuse all work, so the children are idle and the wages of the town fall

questions.explanation: The reasoning is a comparison of who pays for a child nobody keeps: when the parish meets that bill the family has no cost to fear, so the limit on the number of children moves off the household and onto the parish, which is why the writer treats the hospital as the cause and not the cure. The tempting answers make the hospital cheaper to run, blame the family's industry, or suggest the cost falls when it is the parish that carries it.
questions.hint: Ask which household pays when a child does not live.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the state leaves to the household
questions.learningObjective: explain why a law's silence about a household is itself a decision
questions.stem: A thinker argues that the law should not make contracts about marriage and inheritance, because those are the family's own business. What follows for the household?

options.text: The household's own arrangements stand, since the law's silence is a decision to leave property and marriage where they lie

options.misconception: reads silence as absence, when a deliberate silence is a rule
options.text: The household loses all standing, since a law that says nothing leaves every dispute to be settled by force

options.misconception: reads silence as a delay, which turns a decision into a postponement
options.text: The law may still intervene, since a silence is only a delay and a family will always ask the court later

options.misconception: hands the matter to a third body, which is a decision the thinker did not make
options.text: The church decides instead, since marriage and inheritance were always the church's business and not the family's

questions.explanation: A deliberate silence is itself a rule, and it means the household keeps what it has and arranges what it will, so a claim against a wife or an heir is heard where the family hears it and the state has no part in it. The tempting answers read silence as absence, as an invitation to sue later, or as a transfer of the matter to the church, and each of those puts a decision into a silence that was meant to leave none.
questions.hint: A law that says nothing is still doing something. What?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Who gave the consent the law recorded
questions.learningObjective: identify the person the law names as the giver of a valid consent
questions.stem: A marriage is valid only where the party who gives the consent is the one the rule names, and a married woman under the common law gave her consent by her father's act. What does the law identify as the giver?

options.text: The woman's household, since the consent that counted was given by the man whose family she entered

options.misconception: finds a woman who agrees, where the rule names the man of her house
options.text: The woman herself, since the rule asks for her agreement and the father only carried it to court

options.misconception: finds a parish that publishes, which is notice and not consent
options.text: The parish, since a marriage had to be published before a marriage could be binding at all

options.misconception: finds a crown that records, which says nothing about who agreed
options.text: The sovereign, since no subject's consent had weight unless the crown had recorded it as well

questions.explanation: The rule names a giver, and the giver it names is the head of the woman's household, which is why the law in one breath treats her consent as given by her father and treats the marriage as the making of a new household under his roof. The tempting answers find a woman who agrees, a parish that publishes, or a crown that records, and each of those moves the giver away from the person the rule actually names.
questions.hint: The rule says whose consent counts. Ask whose.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where the penalty fell
questions.learningObjective: read a court record as evidence of whom a rule was aimed at
questions.stem: An original summary of a court record from the period reports a case in which the law's consequence was named and applied to a young woman, with nothing said about the man who was with her. What does the record show?

options.text: The law's penalty was aimed at her alone, so the exposure and the disgrace belonged to the woman and the man went free

options.misconception: supplies a property claim the record does not mention
options.text: The young woman had broken a rule of property, so the man was absent because the property was hers to lose

options.misconception: calls a silence a novelty, where the silence is the design of the rule
options.text: The record is a novelty, since a law of that kind usually named both parties and their penalties together

options.misconception: supplies an earlier trial the summary never reports
options.text: The man had been acquitted earlier, so the woman's case was the second half of a trial already decided

questions.explanation: A record that names the person a penalty falls on is reporting the design of the rule as much as the case, and here the design put the exposure and the disgrace on the woman while the man went unmentioned, so the law treated her as the party at fault and him as part of the scene. The tempting answers read the silence as a property claim, as a novelty, or as the tail of a finished trial, and each of those supplies a fact the record does not contain.
questions.hint: Whose name is attached to the penalty in the record?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Headship by agreement
questions.learningObjective: explain what a contract between spouses can and cannot divide
questions.stem: A writer says the husband is head of the household by a contract between the spouses, and denies that the contract gives him any authority over her body. What follows?

options.text: His headship is limited to the household's goods and decisions, so it cannot be read across into her person

options.misconception: empties the contract, so the headship it creates would be a claim with no terms
options.text: His headship is a contract in name only, so every duty he owes her can be set aside when he disagrees

options.misconception: extends the contract past the household, which is the one stretch the writer refuses
options.text: His headship covers her person as well, since a contract between spouses covers whatever they are

options.misconception: denies the contract altogether, which loses the claim the writer was keeping
options.text: The contract is void, since a husband and wife were never free enough to make a contract at all

questions.explanation: A contract is a division of tasks and goods between two parties, so headship by contract means the husband takes a share of the household's decisions and goods and nothing more, and a writer who stops the contract at the household has to stop it before the wife's body. The tempting answers empty the contract, extend it, or deny it altogether, and each of those gives up the one claim the writer was trying to keep.
questions.hint: Ask what a contract between two people can divide between them.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: An answer published as a pamphlet
questions.learningObjective: identify the kind of act a published reply to a charge performs
questions.stem: An original summary reports a woman publishing a long reply to a satire on women's education, and says plainly that the book treated her sex as an insult to it. What is the reply doing?

options.text: Taking the charge as a charge, so she answers the argument and answers it in public rather than asking for leave

options.misconception: turns the reply into a request for retraction, which is not an answer to an argument
options.text: Asking the author to withdraw the satire, so the dispute ends where it started with the man who wrote it

options.misconception: attacks the subject matter rather than the charge, so the charge is left standing
options.text: Offering a different account of learning, so the argument never turns on the insult she was made to suffer

options.misconception: makes the reply a claim to all learning, which is a far larger claim than the book made
options.text: Claiming the whole of learning, so no subject is left to the men who had already written books about it

questions.explanation: Naming the treatment as an insult makes the book a charge against her sex, and a charge can only be answered by an argument, so a reply in print is a way of meeting the case on its own ground instead of seeking leave to speak. The tempting answers turn the reply into a request for retraction, into an attack on the subject matter rather than the charge, or into a claim to all learning, and each of those changes what a published answer to a charge is for.
questions.hint: If the book is a charge, what is the only thing that meets a charge?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A law that ends a penalty and its price
questions.learningObjective: explain what changes first when a penalty on a child is removed
questions.stem: A new law declares a child born outside marriage legitimate on the same terms as any other, and a lawyer works out what the change will do. What does it change first?

options.text: The father's liability, for a penalty on the child was a penalty on the father, so a man may now be bound by what he does

options.misconception: credits the mother's standing, which the child's own treatment was never the route to
options.text: The mother's standing, for a child that was punished drew no notice, so a legitimate child improves her position

options.misconception: counts costs the poor law had borne before, which the change does not touch
options.text: The parish's account, since the poor law had been paying for these children out of the rates for a century

options.misconception: treats the removal of a penalty as a payment, which is a claim about incentives alone
options.text: The rate of births, since a law that removes a penalty is bound to raise the number of children born

questions.explanation: The penalty had been attached to the child in order to reach the father, and it was the threat of that penalty that let a man use the law and walk away, so once the threat is withdrawn the conduct itself has to be governed some other way and the rule that bound nobody now binds the man; the change is a shift in liability, not a rise in births. The tempting answers credit the mother's standing, which the child was never the route to, count the parish's old costs, or assume a penalty's removal is a bribe on the nursery.
questions.hint: Ask who was being punished by the penalty, and why.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The penalty with two addresses
questions.learningObjective: identify the second thing a one-sided penalty also punishes
questions.stem: A law punishes an offence in words that name one person, and in practice the penalty has always been a public disgrace that only one party could feel. What does the record show about that law?

options.text: The penalty was really two things, and the law punished the woman in her body and in her name

options.misconception: makes the penalty a matter of the household, which leaves the two addresses unexplained
options.text: The penalty was meant for the household, so the woman was punished as one of its members and nobody else

options.misconception: denies that the law was enforced, which the record of the cases contradicts
options.text: The penalty was never enforced, so the disgrace a woman felt came from opinion and not from the law

options.misconception: treats a woman's account of the penalty as an exaggeration, which is a verdict and not a reading
options.text: The penalty was too light, so a woman who felt it badly was over-reading a sentence meant to be mild

questions.explanation: When the words name one person and the consequences reach the body and the name of another, the law is punishing two things at once, and the record of the cases shows that the two were not equal, because the exposure and the shame belonged to the woman. The tempting answers make the penalty a matter of the household, deny that it was enforced, or treat a woman's account of it as an exaggeration, and each of those undoes the double meaning the words cannot hide.
questions.hint: Read the punishment, then ask who bore it.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Marriage the court will question
questions.learningObjective: identify the question a law allows a person to raise about a marriage
questions.stem: A law allows a marriage to be set aside where it can be shown that the parties were forced into it, and a woman asks the court to end her own marriage on that ground. What does the law allow her to do?

options.text: Bring the one question a marriage normally closes, since the force is tested by a court and not by the marriage

options.misconception: makes the marriage unanswerable, which is the opposite of what the court is for
options.text: Nothing, since a marriage once made is a matter the parties may not reopen before any judge

options.misconception: confuses the end of a marriage with a change of custody, which is a different suit
options.text: Take the children with her, since a marriage ended for force gives her a claim over the household's goods

options.misconception: treats consent as a word that can be added later, where the law asks whether it was ever given
options.text: Have the marriage blessed, since a forced marriage becomes free the moment both parties say a word

questions.explanation: A law that lets a court set aside a marriage has kept one question outside the marriage, which is whether the parties ever agreed to it, and a woman who brings that question is not reopening the contract but asking the body that made it whether it was ever made. The tempting answers make the marriage unanswerable, confuse the end of a marriage with a change of custody, and treat consent as a word that can be added later.
questions.hint: Which question has the law kept outside the marriage?

questions.topic: Two accounts of where a family's claim comes from
questions.learningObjective: compare two accounts of the footing of a parent's claim
questions.stem: Two original summaries meet: one says a father has a right to the child because he has fed it, the other says a father has no right at all because a child belongs to no man. Which synthesis fits both?

options.text: One states the claim as the facts give it and the other denies that any such claim is natural, so the dispute is about its source

options.misconception: splits the two by sex, which neither summary does
options.text: One is a father's account of his duty and the other a mother's account of her right, and they are about different people

options.misconception: splits the two by written law and custom, and neither names either
options.text: One stands for law as it was written and the other for custom as families kept it, so the two cannot be compared

options.misconception: makes them differ over a signature, which is a detail neither summary raises
options.text: Both hold that a father may be bound to his child, differing only in whether the mother must also agree

questions.explanation: The two summaries take the same event, a father with a child, and give it a different footing, one resting on the care that has been given and the other refusing to let nature supply a claim at all, so the disagreement is about where such a claim comes from and not about the child. The tempting answers split the two by sex, or by written law and custom, or make them differ over a mother's agreement, and each of those leaves the two accounts agreeing about the ground they are arguing over.
questions.hint: The summaries differ in the footing, not in the family.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A bargain made for a case the theory left empty
questions.learningObjective: explain why a rule about a child can rest on an agreement rather than nature
questions.stem: A writer argues that a child born to a slave mother is bound to serve the child of the master, and he admits that the bond is a bargain rather than a natural one. Explain the reason given.

options.text: A natural right to the child belongs to nobody there, so the rule fills the empty place with an agreement that runs to the master

options.misconception: puts the first duty with the mother, which restores a right the author had taken away
options.text: A child's first duty is to the mother who bore it, so the bargain must be made with her and not with the master

options.misconception: makes the service natural, which is what the author expressly denies by calling it a bargain
options.text: A child's nature fixes its service, so the bargain records a fact that holds whether or not anyone agrees

options.misconception: makes it a paid contract the child may leave, which no account of the bond allows
options.text: The master pays wages, so the bond is a contract of pay like any other and the child may leave it

questions.explanation: The writer says the bond is a bargain because his own account of what belongs to people by nature leaves the child unclaimed, and a rule that leaves a place empty is usually filled by a contract, so the agreement is what gives the child to the master. The tempting answers put the first duty with the mother, make the service natural, or make it a paid contract the child may leave, and each of those restores a right or a choice the author had expressly taken away.
questions.hint: Why is it a bargain? Look for the absence the bargain fills.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The answer that gives away the principle
questions.learningObjective: spot when a limiting answer grants the principle it was meant to limit
questions.stem: A writer asks why a person born in one country is not a citizen of it, and the answer given is that the child was born in another country. What does that answer do?

options.text: It grants the principle it was meant to limit, since a birth decides membership by place rather than by any choice

options.misconception: treats a rule about a child's age as an answer about a child's country
options.text: It limits the principle properly, because a child cannot be asked to choose a country before it can speak

options.misconception: denies the state's right, which is a different dispute from the one asked
options.text: It denies the principle outright, on the ground that no state may decide who its citizens are

options.misconception: calls a fact unweighable, which leaves the rule standing without answering it
options.text: It leaves the principle open, since where a child was born is a fact no law is able to weigh

questions.explanation: The answer is meant to show that the claim is odd, and it does the opposite, because a rule that gives a child citizenship by the accident of where it was born accepts that membership can be settled by place, which is the very claim it was meant to refuse. The tempting answers read it as a sensible limit for a child too young to choose, as a denial of the state's right, or as a question no law can weigh, and none of them is what a place of birth decides.
questions.hint: What does a rule about the place of birth assume?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Consent given and consent kept
questions.learningObjective: identify the limit a philosopher places on a parent's right
questions.stem: A philosopher says a parent's right to a child lasts only while the child needs the parent, and compares it with a loan rather than a purchase. What is the claim?

options.text: The right is a trust for the child's sake, so it ends when the child can direct its own life

options.misconception: turns the trust into a sale, which is the very comparison the writer refuses
options.text: The right is a purchase, so the child is bought and may be sold on when the buyer chooses

options.misconception: makes the right the child's from the start, which the comparison of a loan denies
options.text: The right belongs to the child, so a parent who uses it for itself has taken the child's property

options.misconception: makes it a gift without an end, which a loan can never be
options.text: The right is a gift that cannot be ended, so a child remains the parent's whatever the child does

questions.explanation: The comparison with a loan fixes the length of the right by the need it meets, and a loan of that kind is handed over for the borrower's sake and is not the lender's to keep, so the parent's claim ends where the child's own direction begins. The tempting answers turn the trust into a sale, into a right the child already holds, or into a gift that cannot be withdrawn, and each of those gives the parent more time than the comparison allows.
questions.hint: How long does a loan last, and who does it serve?

questions.topic: The comparison that settles the argument
questions.learningObjective: explain what a fair test requires before a comparison can be used
questions.stem: A reformer argues that a difference between men's and women's achievements is settled by giving women the same schooling and then measuring the result. What is the force of the argument?

options.text: It takes the difference as a question, and a fair test decides it, so the schooling must be equal before a result means anything

options.misconception: turns the test into a poll, which counts opinions instead of comparing results
options.text: It settles the difference by a vote, so the number that agrees with the reformer is the finding of the inquiry

options.misconception: assumes the conclusion, which the order of the argument carefully avoids
options.text: It assumes the answer, since a reformer who begins by calling the sexes alike has already decided the question

options.misconception: loads the test, so the comparison never becomes fair and cannot decide anything
options.text: It puts the burden on women, since an untested capacity is theirs to prove before the claim is heard

questions.explanation: The argument borrows the method the new sciences had made ordinary, which is to hold the conditions equal and then measure, and the measure is what makes the result worth having, so the schooling has to be the same before the comparison can be used against anyone. The tempting answers turn the test into a poll, assume the conclusion at the start, or hand the burden of proof to the half being measured, and each of those replaces the experiment with something else.
questions.hint: What has to be the same before a comparison can be used?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A measure against a sphere
questions.learningObjective: synthesize an assigned sphere with a demand that differences be tested
questions.stem: Two original summaries meet: one says a woman's life has its own sphere, the other says a difference must be measured before it is accepted as natural. Which synthesis fits both?

options.text: The first offers a world the second has not looked at, and the second has not looked at it, so the two do not meet until one is tested

options.misconception: makes the two instruments unusable together, which is a result and not a reading of them
options.text: The first assigns a place and the second disputes the measuring, so the two together leave a woman without a sphere or a test

options.misconception: calls them one claim, when one assigns and the other questions
options.text: The summaries are the same claim twice, since a sphere of one's own is the plainest kind of measure of a life

options.misconception: settles the question in advance by calling every difference natural
options.text: The second settles the matter, since a natural difference must show itself equally in every age and place

questions.explanation: The two summaries do not describe the same world, because the first has already assigned the woman a region and the second is asking whether any difference there is a difference of kind or of condition, so the measure and the sphere cannot both be in place until one of them is examined. The tempting answers make them two ways of saying the same thing, leave a woman without either instrument, or settle the question in advance by calling every difference natural.
questions.hint: What would each summary have to concede for the other to work?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The home as a school of duty
questions.learningObjective: explain why unpaid work in a household can be described as training
questions.stem: A moral textbook tells a boy that his sisters' care of the household is a training for their future duties as wives and mothers. What is the reasoning?

options.text: The family's work teaches those duties, so the boy's own schooling is to learn his part in the same household economy

options.misconception: turns training into wages, which is a claim the text does not make
options.text: The family's work earns them keep, so a girl who serves the household is paid a share of what it earns

options.misconception: turns training into a property claim, which is a different claim again
options.text: The family's work proves a claim, so a girl who serves the household is owed a portion when she leaves

options.misconception: turns training into a lesson in command, and the boy is asked to learn not to serve
options.text: The family's work is a lesson in power, so the boy is taught to command the household he will one day head

questions.explanation: The textbook treats the household as a training ground and so reads a daughter's unpaid work as instruction for the duties named, which is why the boy is asked to learn his own part of the same economy rather than to command it. The tempting answers turn the work into wages, into a share of the property, or into a lesson in authority, and each of those replaces the training the text describes with a claim of the boy's own.
questions.hint: Is the work being described as pay, as a claim, or as training?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reader the rule approved
questions.learningObjective: infer what a rule prefers from the reader it names as an example
questions.stem: A rule allows a book to be printed if a reader is paid to read it and report on it, and the rule's own example of the proper reader is a man who does not go out. What does the rule prefer?

options.text: A reader already at home, so a book is judged by someone with no occasion to be in company or the streets

options.misconception: makes fame the criterion, which the example of one reader at home does not supply
options.text: A reader who is known, so a book's character is taken from the opinion of people of established name

options.misconception: makes leisure the criterion, which is close to the truth but not what the example turns on
options.text: A reader with time, so a long book is judged by the man who can afford to sit with it for weeks

options.misconception: makes payment the criterion, which is a fact of the arrangement and not of the reader
options.text: A reader who is paid, so a book is judged by the man whose judgement the rule has already bought

questions.explanation: The rule's own example describes a man of leisure who stays within his own walls, and that is the reader whose opinion can be had without mixing him with anyone else, which tells us the rule is choosing the man least likely to be changed by what he reads. The tempting answers make the criterion fame, time, or payment, and each of those misses the stillness in the example the rule itself gives.
questions.hint: What does the rule's own example say about where the reader is?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The room the town disliked
questions.learningObjective: identify what a council is really objecting to in a leisure complaint
questions.stem: A town council complains that the tavern is where the wage is spent, and asks that the licences be pulled in. What is the council actually objecting to?

options.text: The company the wage buys, since a room where the day's pay is discussed is where a wage can be questioned

options.misconception: names drink, which is a complaint the council could make without thinking about wages
options.text: The drink itself, since a council that has been asked about the wages may reasonably suspect the cup

options.misconception: names competition, which has nothing to do with what is said in the room
options.text: The competition, since a tavern draws custom from shops the council would rather see full of buyers

options.misconception: names revenue, which is a motive the council would not have to say out loud
options.text: The tax, since licences are the one revenue the council can raise without asking the town's permission

questions.explanation: A council watching a wage complain that it is spent in one room is not objecting to beer but to the company that comes with it, because a room where the day's pay is named and compared is where a wage can be questioned instead of obeyed, so the licence is the thing to pull and the grievance is political. The tempting answers name drink, competition and taxation, and each of those is a complaint the council could make without ever thinking about what its workpeople say in the room.
questions.hint: What else happens in the room where the pay is spent?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the employer must pay above the day's bread
questions.learningObjective: explain why a low wage defeats the bargain it is meant to buy
questions.stem: An employer argues that a workman who earns barely enough for his family's food cannot be got to do a full day's work, and that the family will not let him. Explain the reasoning.

options.text: The wage is compared with the family's subsistence, so paying less than that ends the bargain and the day's work is not bought

options.misconception: measures the wage against beer, which the employer had no reason to mention
options.text: The wage is compared with the price of beer, so paying less than that leaves a man too tired to finish his shift

options.misconception: measures it against the master's own pay, which is a complaint about the share and not the rate
options.text: The wage is compared with the master's own pay, so paying less shows that the master has set the work above its worth

options.misconception: measures it against the parish allowance, which is a rule and not a family's food
options.text: The wage is compared with the rate the parish allows, so paying more keeps a family off the poor roll

questions.explanation: The argument is about what the family will agree to, not about the man's stomach: a wage that does not cover the family's subsistence is a wage the family refuses, so the employer who pays it cannot have the labour and the low rate saves nothing. The tempting answers measure the wage against beer, against the master's own pay, or against the parish's allowance, and none of those is the sum a household has to find before a man will leave the house.
questions.hint: Whose decision about the wage is the employer waiting for?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The part of the plan that is actually scarce
questions.learningObjective: identify the input a generous offer cannot buy
questions.stem: A town wants more engineers, and a rich man offers to buy the machines, hire the site, and pay the first year's wages. What is missing from the plan?

options.text: The teachers, since machines and money cannot train a person, and the training is the part the offer leaves out

options.misconception: asks for material, which is one of the things the offer already covers
options.text: The raw material, since the machines will stand idle until a local mine can supply what they work on

options.misconception: asks for a buyer, which money can also obtain
options.text: The market, since the engineers must be paid from a sale that the plan provides no buyer for

options.misconception: asks for a right, which is also something the plan could buy
options.text: The patent, since the law requires the owner of a machine to hold the right before any man may work it

questions.explanation: Machines, a site and a first wage buy the things that can be bought, and what the plan lacks is the part that cannot be, which is the teaching that turns a boy into an engineer, so the offer is generous and still leaves the binding constraint untouched. The tempting answers ask for material, a market or a patent, and each of those is something money can obtain, which is exactly the class of thing the offer already covers.
questions.hint: Which part of the plan could no money in the plan buy?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A critique that is half right
questions.learningObjective: separate a measurable claim in a critique from one that is not
questions.stem: A writer says the age of invention is over because the goods are consumed as fast as they are made, and that the workers have become pieces of machinery rather than craftsmen. What stands?

options.text: The share of what is made reaches the workman, a share that can be counted, but the loss of craft is a claim about skill

options.misconception: throws away both halves, which the writer's evidence does not require
options.text: Neither half stands, because invention follows consumption and will stop when the market is full

options.misconception: turns the second half into a complaint about pay, which is a different question
options.text: The first half stands and the second is a complaint about pay, since skill is what a worker is paid for

options.misconception: makes the first half cause the second, which is an order the writer never gave
options.text: Both stand together, because a worker who has lost his craft will soon have nothing left to sell

questions.explanation: The critique has two claims and they are not the same kind, because the share of the product that reaches the worker is a matter of account and can be stated, while the loss of craft is a claim about what the work now asks of a man, and no account of shares will show it. The tempting answers throw both away, turn the second into a complaint about pay, or make the first cause the second, and each of those refuses the one distinction the critique turns on.
questions.hint: Which of the two claims is a matter of account?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A week of hours at two mills
questions.learningObjective: read a labour return as a claim about the length of the working day
questions.stem: An inspector's return for one week shows one mill at ten hours a day for six days, and another at six hours a day for the same six days, with the same fifty hands at both. What does the return show?

options.text: That the same work was bought with three fifths of the hours, and the argument over the long day is a claim about quantity

options.misconception: confuses fewer hours with better work, which the return does not show
options.text: That the second mill was more efficient, since the same hands finished in fewer hours what the first took ten a day to start

options.misconception: reads contentment into an inspector's return, which records hours and nothing else
options.text: That the long day suited the men better, so the inspector's figures show the week was a happy one for the hands

options.misconception: makes the two totals incommensurable, which lets the rule go without an answer
options.text: That the two mills were measuring different work, so the totals cannot be compared and the rule settles nothing

questions.explanation: The second mill bought the same hands and the same six days for thirty-six hours where the first bought sixty, and thirty-six is three fifths of sixty, so two fifths of the labour time went without any change in the goods. The tempting answers confuse fewer hours with better work, read contentment into an inspector's return, or make the two totals incommensurable, and each of those forgets that the rule under dispute is a rule about quantity.
questions.hint: Thirty-six against sixty is a fraction. Which one?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The objection that widens the target
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an objection about a symptom from one about its cause
questions.stem: A regulation is argued for on the ground that no soldier should be found in an inn, and a writer objects that the fault is not the drink but the hours. What does the objection show?

options.text: That the real fault is the time that leaves a man idle enough to want the room, so this is not the remedy argued for

options.misconception: agrees with the rule and moves the remedy, which is not what the objection did
options.text: That soldiers drink only when they are idle, so the rule is right and the hours are what should be changed

options.misconception: defends the room itself, which is a different claim from the one the writer made
options.text: That the inn is a better school of duty than the barracks, so the objection is really a defence of drink

options.misconception: attacks a word in the regulation instead of the remedy the writer objected to
options.text: That an inn is not a public house, so the regulation was written about the wrong building at some point

questions.explanation: The objection takes the example and asks what produced it, and if the fault is that the hours leave a man with time to want the room, then a rule about the room treats the symptom and leaves the cause, which is what makes the objection a criticism of the remedy rather than of the men. The tempting answers agree with the rule and change the hours instead, defend the inn on its own merits, or insist the rule was aimed at the wrong building.
questions.hint: Ask what the long hours and the room have to do with one another.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Leisure as a trade and as a duty
questions.learningObjective: synthesize a costing of leisure with a standard set for it
questions.stem: Two original summaries meet: one says the new comforts turned leisure into a trade that sells hours back to the people who buy them, the other says the new comforts made leisure a duty to be improved. Which synthesis fits both?

options.text: One counts what leisure now costs and the other what it is for, so the same hours can be a purchase and a task at once

options.misconception: makes the two exclusive, when they answer different questions about the same afternoons
options.text: The summaries are rivals, since a trade in hours and a duty to improve cannot be true of the same people

options.misconception: settles the question in favour of the second, which the pair does not allow
options.text: The second settles the matter, because a leisure that improves is a better use than a leisure that is sold

options.misconception: reads both as one complaint about a lost taste, which neither summary makes
options.text: Both are complaints about the same decline, since no one who worked all day had a taste for the theatre

questions.explanation: The two summaries are answering different questions about the same afternoons, one asking what leisure now costs the worker and the other asking what the worker is expected to do with it, and nothing in the first prevents the hours from being sold and nothing in the second forbids their being sold, so a leisure can be a purchase and an improvement at the same time. The tempting answers make the two exclusive, settle the question in favour of the second, or read both as one complaint about a lost taste, and each of those closes a comparison the summaries leave open.
questions.hint: What question is each summary actually asking?
